Health authorities dispatched teams to the affected village to assess household contacts and monitor residents; all contacted family members were reported healthy. The Centre for Health Protection is conducting epidemiological investigations and will report the case to the World Health Organization. This marks another local monkeypox case detected in Hong Kong.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue Fever and Acute Respiratory Infections Threaten Children as the Seasons Change
article.articleSummary: Jakarta-based pediatric specialist Mulki Angela warns that the transition from dry to rainy season raises risks of acute respiratory infections (ARI), including influenza A, particularly in Jakarta. Smoke from forest-fire/peatland fires (karhutla) areas can exacerbate respiratory problems. With the onset of rain, dengue fever (DBD) transmission risk increases due to mosquitoes. Limited access to clean water may cause diarrheal illness and vomiting, and skin infections can occur. Preventive measures focus on 3M Plus for dengue, regular handwashing, bathing, changing clothes, maintaining a clean home, and eliminating standing water; ensure adequate fluids for children and have fever-reducing medicines at home. To bolster immunity, emphasize balanced nutrition, physical activity, sleep, and possibly vitamin D supplementation. Transmission precautions include distancing from the sick, masking, coughing etiquette, and ensuring complete immunizations. Parents should prepare children’s rain gear and spare clothes for wet conditions.

article.articleHeadline: Evidence of widespread sequencing errors in global avian influenza study
article.articleSummary: As of 2 November 2026, concerns over Wannigama et al. (2025) arise from a global avian influenza study using guano samples from Africa (Madagascar, Mozambique, Somalia), the Middle East (Yemen), South Asia (Maldives, Sri Lanka), Southeast Asia (Indonesia, Myanmar, the Philippines) and Oceania (Papua New Guinea). While aiming to fill surveillance gaps and inform high-pathogenicity avian influenza (HPAI) incursion risk, the study’s sequences and conclusions clash with established influenza evolution. Key issues include 100% identity of HA and NA segments across disparate regions and years, which is implausible for rapidly evolving influenza A viruses with clock-like mutation rates (~1.8–8.4×10^-3 substitutions/site/year). Root-to-tip analyses (TempEst) reveal outliers; phylogenies show H7 and H5N1 sequences (PNG, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Mozambique) from 2021–2022 identical to an eradicated Australian H7N7, and PNG sequences identical to older GISAID records (2004–2018). Data quality problems in GenBank/GISAID hinder interpretation, risk assessments, and policy decisions.

article.articleHeadline: Stopping bird flu beyond the farm
article.articleSummary: Avian influenza, H5N1, remains a threat to poultry, livelihoods, and public health across Asia and the Pacific. In March, H5N1-positive poultry in Cambodia triggered investigations that identified a human infection; in June Australia confirmed H5N1 in a migratory seabird, illustrating cross-border spread across farms, wildlife, and the environment. The UN General Assembly’s Oct 12 Political Declaration urges pandemic prevention via a One Health approach linking human, animal, and environmental health, while climate variability and stronger El Niño (peaking late 2026 per WMO) may raise disease risks and drive farm runoff spreading pathogens. FAO-supported work in Cambodia, Indonesia, and Sulawesi demonstrates surveillance and risk reduction. Three priorities: (1) integrate wildlife/environmental data with animal/human surveillance; (2) invest in frontline, laboratory capacity; (3) embed upstream prevention with sustained funding in national plans. One Health Day emphasizes coordinated prevention.

article.articleHeadline: Melioidosis in Thailand: Soil Fever Explained
article.articleSummary: Melioidosis, or soil fever, is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei and is endemic in Thailand, with especially high risk in the Northeast and eastern regions (Chiang Rai cited). The bacteria enter via skin cuts, swallowing contaminated water, or inhalation of disturbed soil or water; person-to-person transmission is rare. Symptoms can include fever, cough, breathing problems, or skin abscesses, typically appearing 1–4 weeks after exposure, though delays of months or years are possible. Diagnosis relies on cultures. Treatment requires an initial intensive antibiotic course followed by a prolonged oral regimen. Rainy-season outdoor work increases exposure risk, and untreated well or natural water may pose additional danger. Preventive measures include wearing boots, covering wounds, and drinking treated water. A 2025 study reported melioidosis in 36 of 1,486 adults admitted with bacterial pneumonia in an endemic region.

article.articleHeadline: Discovery of visceral leishmaniasis from an armpit ulcer.
article.articleSummary: On 2026-11-02 in Hanoi, a 67-year-old woman (Bà Minh) presented with 40°C fever, headache, cough progressing to pneumonia and respiratory failure. An axillary ulcer with a black eschar and round red lesions on the face and forearm were observed. She had garden exposure two weeks earlier. Diagnostic workup for scrub typhus—caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by chiggers—included blood cultures and biochemical tests; she was diagnosed with scrub typhus and treated with targeted antibiotics. After three days, fever abated and fatigue improved, though diarrhea persisted, prompting a regimen change. After a week of intensified therapy, pneumonia and liver enzyme elevations improved. The report notes that scrub typhus can resemble other febrile illnesses (flu, COVID-19, dengue) and that black eschars may appear at hidden bite sites such as the armpit, groin, or under the breast. Gardening or outdoor exposure is a key risk factor.

article.articleHeadline: The danger posed by the RSV virus to children and effective prevention methods.
article.articleSummary: RSV, the respiratory syncytial virus, is a common cause of lower respiratory infection in Vietnam children, potentially causing bronchiolitis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure, especially in infants under 2 years (notably under 6 months) or those with congenital heart or lung disease. It spreads mainly through droplets and contaminated surfaces and circulates year-round with seasonal peaks. At Thanh Son Regional Medical Center, Pediatrics reports multiple RSV admissions. Early symptoms include runny nose, congestion, cough, mild fever, irritability, and poor feeding; progression can lead to bronchiolitis or pneumonia with rapid breathing, wheeze, and chest retractions. Severe disease risks respiratory failure; warning signs include tachypnea, chest indrawing, cyanosis, poor feeding, lethargy, or apnea. Immunity is not long-lasting, so reinfections occur. Prevention emphasizes hand hygiene, cleaning surfaces and toys, avoiding sick contacts and tobacco smoke, ventilated spaces, and avoiding crowds. Some high-risk children may receive monoclonal antibodies as prophylaxis after physician assessment. A case: 8-day-old girl with cyanosis and lung collapse due to RSV.

From 11 June to 30 October 2026 ASF affected 32 households across 10 of 18 hamlets, causing the death and culling of 1,217 pigs, totaling 92.37 tons. The commune responded by zoning, culling infected animals, reinforcing disinfection and environmental sanitation, and conducting public education. The inspection focused on assessing the outbreak status, addressing difficulties, and proposing measures to control the disease, minimize losses, and prevent further spread. It urged strict outbreak surveillance, tighter control of all pig-keeping households, enhanced hygiene, and enforcement of prevention regulations. Officials were asked to strengthen accountability, monitoring, reporting, and public communication, with a goal to suppress outbreaks by 15 November 2026 and declare the outbreak over by 25 November 2026.

article.articleHeadline: 27-month-old girl in critical condition due to dengue fever complications
article.articleSummary: 27-month-old girl from Thanh Hóa, Vietnam, with dengue fever developed fulminant myocarditis and cardiogenic shock, saved after nearly five weeks on VA-ECMO at Ho Chi Minh City Children's Hospital. NS1-positive dengue; within 12 hours she deteriorated to respiratory failure and shock requiring resuscitation. Echocardiography showed EF down to 28–30%, then 24–26%, indicating severe systolic dysfunction. Diagnosed with dengue-associated fulminant myocarditis and liver injury; transferred to ICU. VA-ECMO support with ventilation, inotropes, and multi-organ supportive care; eight sessions of continuous dialysis were required. After ~5 weeks, cardiac function improved (EF 48–52%), blood pressure stabilized; weaning from ECMO and ventilation followed. After ~2 months, sinus rhythm returned, liver and kidney function recovered, urine output improved. This is a rare dengue-related fulminant myocarditis case; parents urged to seek early care for warning signs. Local dengue activity: week of Oct 19–25 had 1,785 cases; year-to-date 42,515; Con Dao, Ngai Giao, Minh Thanh high incidence.

article.articleHeadline: Child in critical condition after influenza infection; doctors warn of abnormal signs.
article.articleSummary: Eight children at Vietnam's National Children’s Hospital have developed severe complications after influenza infection, including three deaths; five remain in critical condition as of November 2, 2026. Hospitalizations for influenza A are rising. Beyond respiratory illness, influenza can trigger myocarditis, necrotizing encephalitis, and acute encephalopathy following infection (ITES). ITES denotes a group of acute brain disorders occurring during or after infection and may be linked to influenza and other viruses; brain injury may arise from post-infectious immune responses rather than direct viral invasion. A rare but serious neurological complication, acute necrotizing encephalopathy (ANE), can follow days of fever and respiratory symptoms and present with altered consciousness, drowsiness, seizures, or coma. There is no universally effective targeted therapy; management is primarily supportive, focusing on seizure control, brain edema, and multidisciplinary care. Parents should seek urgent care for fever with seizures or rapid mental-status decline.

article.articleHeadline: Heat, Smog and Mosquitoes: How Climate Change Is Making India Sick, Says Lancet Report
article.articleSummary: Heat, smog and mosquitoes drive rising climate-health risks in India, per the Lancet Countdown. In 2023, heat caused a record 7.1 lakh deaths globally, with 71.5% linked to human-caused climate change. India faces about 2,600 hours/year of heat stress and little night relief, with 64 hours of sleep lost annually (2021–25). Among medium-HDI countries, India bears the highest heat-stress burden (~2,430 hours/person/year) and heat deaths total about 1.26%, with 56.3% attributed to climate change. PM2.5 pollution killed about 2.2 million in India in 2023, worth US$517 billion. Mosquito-borne risks rise: transmission potential for Aedes vectors increases; malaria transmission months up 19% for Pf and 18% for Pv (2016–25 vs 1981–90). Vibrio coastline suitability expands 27% to ~2,740 km by 2025. Outdoor workers face substantial global GDP losses.

article.articleHeadline: What will happen if you drink milk from a cow afflicted with rabies? Clear your confusion about the rabies virus.
article.articleSummary: Rabies is a fatal Lyssavirus infection transmitted from animals to humans. In India, rabies cases are high due to stray dogs, though other animals can also be infected. Regarding dairy from an afflicted cow, India’s National Rabies Control Programme finds no evidence that milk from rabid cows spreads rabies, and there is no scientific proof that dairy products pose a risk. Nonetheless, safety precautions are advised and such milk is not considered completely safe to consume. The WHO likewise reports no evidence of transmission via dairy products from infected animals but recommends avoiding these products. Boiling milk or pasteurization inactivates the virus, given its heat sensitivity. Fermentation-based dairy products (e.g., yogurt, cheese) should not be viewed as substitutes for heating. For health concerns, consult a doctor.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue risk persists even after the monsoon! Learn prevention and recovery tips from an expert.
article.articleSummary: Dengue risk persists after the monsoon even as the season ends, because residual humidity and standing water sustain mosquitoes. Recent dengue cases underscore the ongoing threat. Symptoms typically appear 4–10 days after infection and include sudden high fever, severe headache behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and a skin rash; platelets may fall, causing weakness. Not all low platelets indicate severity, but medical evaluation with blood tests is essential. Urgent care signs include persistent abdominal pain, continuous vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, restlessness, rapid breathing, or clammy skin. Prevention focuses on eliminating mosquito breeding sites and bite avoidance: remove standing water around home (rooftops, pots, coolers); cover water tanks; wear long sleeves in parks; apply repellents. Recovery priorities are rest, hydration (boiled water, ORS, coconut water, soups), and easily digestible nutrition (khichdi, dal, greens, fruit, protein). Narayana Hospital, Gurugram, Dr. M.K. Singh emphasizes vigilance after monsoon.

article.articleHeadline: Five overlooked steps to identify new epidemics, fast
article.articleSummary: Five overlooked steps to identify new epidemics, fast article argues that early detection remains hard as novel pathogens present atypical symptoms. Outbreaks discussed include the Ebola epidemic in Africa, the ongoing global threats from COVID-19, mpox, hantavirus; SARS-CoV-2 in 2020 had fever and respiratory distress, mpox 2022 in Europe and North America featured genital/anal sores, Nipah virus circulating in Bangladesh and India showing brain inflammation or breathing difficulties. Surveillance currently relies on event-based tracking, genomic sequencing, and syndromic surveillance, but atypical presentations can delay recognition. The authors propose five steps forming a symptom-preparedness loop: flag clusters of unusual cases using reporting procedures and DHIS2; use AI to flag atypical cases; adopt tiered case definitions (suspected/probable/confirmed) updated regularly. Tech tools include DHIS2 and centralized AI systems; aim to speed frontline alerts and public-health response.

article.articleHeadline: Bhopal coughs, labs have no answers: Is it pollution or a changing flu strain?
article.articleSummary: Bhopal, India, 2 November 2026 — Prolonged cough, cold and fever are increasingly common among patients visiting OPDs in Bhopal. The State Virology Laboratory at Gandhi Medical College (GMC) has not conducted genome sequencing and has passed responsibility to AIIMS Bhopal, leaving uncertainty about whether a changing flu strain or other respiratory pathogens are driving the surge. Some doctors privately suspect seasonal influenza, including H1N1, though no circulating strain has been confirmed by sequencing. AIIMS Bhopal has been approached for clarification and has not yet responded. GMC Pomnologist Dr Vikas Gupta attributed the pattern to significant temperature variations and environmental factors from rapid construction, Metro rail work, and urban development, with dust exposure and changing weather contributing to flu-like infections. Many patients and coughing episodes are reported in crowded spaces, including cinema halls. Precautionary guidance urged for those predisposed to respiratory illnesses; ideal genome sequencing to guide preventive measures.

They cited Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD), or monkey fever, in Karnataka—where cases continue to be missed despite mortality declines in Shivamogga—and noted the first human death from the animal-borne Shamonda virus. Calls were made to recognize gram panchayats as One Health stakeholders, prioritize resource allocation, and integrate milk and meat production considerations. Although advanced technology exists, deployment mechanisms are lacking; village- and ward-level committees showed value during COVID-19 and should be expanded. Emphasis was placed on system-based SOPs, improved information-sharing among departments, and collaboration with local organizations to strengthen surveillance and response.

article.articleHeadline: Climate change: More than a thousand chickens died suddenly in poultry farms.
article.articleSummary: More than 1,000 chickens suddenly died at poultry farms in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu, notably in Tiruchopuram near the coast, with affected sites including Thamanampettai and Kurinjipadi. The mass mortality occurred in the days leading up to Diwali, as birds were being prepared for sale. The Department of Animal Husbandry, led by Joint Director Murugavel, Assistant Director Venkatalakshmi, and veterinary officers, visited farms in Thamanampettai and nearby areas to assess husbandry practices, farm sanitation, feed, and drinking-water supplies. Samples have been collected to determine whether deaths result from an infectious disease, climate-related stress from erratic monsoon conditions (northeast monsoon, alternating rain and sun) and a Bay of Bengal cyclone causing rainfall, or other factors. Lab results are pending. Separately, residents report fever, cough, and cold amid fluctuating weather conditions, signaling potential public health implications from the weather pattern.

article.articleHeadline: Man's both legs scratched by rice straw, nearly died; leptospirosis to blame.
article.articleSummary: In Shenzhen, Guangdong, a 24-year-old man developed leptospirosis after returning to Hunan to harvest rice; his legs were cut by rice straw, and both the home and fields harbored rats. Starting Oct 31, he experienced fever up to 38.1°C for five days, with severe headache, back and lower-limb muscle pain, and nausea with vomiting, making it hard to lie down. No waterproof boots were worn while working in the fields. Laboratory testing detected Leptospira in the kidney, with sequence type 1007, confirming leptospirosis (Weil's disease). Major reservoirs include rats, pigs, cattle and sheep; humans acquire infection through contact with contaminated water or soil or direct contact with blood or urine from infected animals. Early symptoms resemble influenza; severe disease can cause pulmonary hemorrhage, jaundice, liver and kidney failure, and be life-threatening. After antibiotics and platelet transfusion, the patient recovered and was discharged.

article.articleHeadline: Beijing CDC: Why is norovirus easily transmitted on campus, and what should schools and parents do?
article.articleSummary: Norovirus is highly contagious and rapidly spreads in dense settings such as Beijing schools and childcare facilities. Transmission is fecal-oral via close contact with an infected person, contaminated objects, vomiting aerosols, or contaminated food or water. Onset is typically 12–48 hours after exposure; symptoms are vomiting and diarrhea and usually last 2–3 days, with possible reinfection. Prevention emphasizes hand hygiene, boiled water, thoroughly cooked foods, washing fruits and vegetables, and avoiding raw or undercooked items. Infected individuals should stay home to limit spread. Parents should teach children good handwashing before meals, ensure rest and nutrition, and cooperate with schools for stool testing if GI symptoms occur; disinfect with chlorine-based agents and boil utensils for 30 minutes during home isolation. Schools should perform daily health checks, reporting, and environmental disinfection; cafeteria staff who test positive must be off duty until two consecutive negative Norovirus PCR tests, 24 hours apart, and outbreaks reported to local CDC and school health offices.

article.articleHeadline: China CDC: The reported incidence rate of infectious diarrhea among elderly people aged 60 and above in China is on the rise.
article.articleSummary: China CDC Weekly reports rising infectious diarrhea incidence among adults aged 60+ from 2005–2025, with about 2.58 million cases. The incidence increased from 31.27 per 100,000 in 2005 to 91.74 per 100,000 in 2025; risk rises with age, highest in 85+ individuals. Viral pathogens predominate (Norovirus, Rotavirus); bacterial pathogens include Salmonella and Vibrio parahaemolyticus. Diarrhea occurs year-round, with peaks in July–August; cases are more common in eastern and southern coastal provinces, notably Shandong, Anhui, Zhejiang, Guangdong, and Henan. Warmer, humid environments and higher seafood consumption may boost exposure to foodborne pathogens. Norovirus—highly contagious, environmentally stable, and rapidly genetically variable—drives many elderly-care facility outbreaks. Deployment of nationwide smart infectious disease surveillance improves reporting timeliness and completeness. Recommendations: strengthen surveillance, food safety regulation, and pathogen detection, especially in summer/fall and high-incidence areas; prioritize 85+ elderly and elderly-care facility staff for interventions.

article.articleHeadline: Zhucheng Releases Guidelines for Public Reporting of Clues Related to Infectious Disease Outbreaks
article.articleSummary: Zhucheng City announces guidelines for public reporting of clues related to infectious disease outbreaks, under the PRC Infectious Disease Prevention and Control Law. Reporting triggers include: (1) severe illness or death after close contact with poultry, livestock, or wildlife; (2) returnees from high-incidence countries/regions with fever, cough, rash, diarrhea, or vomiting; (3) a cluster (five or more) with similar symptoms within a week in a community, workplace, school, home, or venue; (4) abnormal events in border areas, endemic foci, or areas with active vectors or unusual animal deaths; (5) other public health risks. Channel: Zhucheng CDC 24-hour duty line 0536-6212583. Reports should be factual, confidential, protective measures taken, and individuals urged to seek formal medical care and disclose exposure history. article.articleHeadline: DH announces latest situation regarding Legionnaires' disease cases
article.articleSummary: Six community-acquired Legionnaires' disease cases were reported Oct 25–31 in Hong Kong, all male, aged 48–78 (Wan Chai, Yau Tsim Mong, Southern, Sha Tin, Tai Po). No epidemiological links to prior cases; CHP is investigating potential infection sources; cases are sporadic. By Oct 31, 169 LD cases in 2026; 2025 had 167; 2024 135. Risk factors: male, over 50, smoking, immunocompromised; environmental risks include poorly maintained water systems, cooling towers, fountains, hot-water systems, whirlpool spas, hotels or ships. Legionella thrives in warm water (20–45 C) in tanks, piping, humidifiers, and home devices; infection via inhalation of aerosols. Guidance for immunocompromised: sterile or boiled water for drinking/oral care; avoid humidifiers or use sterile water; clean regularly; drain stagnant water. Public advice: hygiene, avoid smoking/alcohol, inspect and clean taps/shower outlets; 0.2 µm filters if used; quarterly tank drainage; purge outlets weekly. Smoking cessation hotline 1833 183.

article.articleHeadline: Is the Danger Next Door at Our Doorstep? West Nile Virus Warnings from Dr. Ramazan İnci
article.articleSummary: West Nile Virus (WNV) warnings. As cases rise in Greece and Europe, Turkey faces potential risk. Transmission: birds serve as reservoirs and Culex mosquitoes are the main vectors; infection occurs when an infected mosquito bites a person. WNV has been reported across Africa, Europe, the Middle East, North America and West Asia, with outbreaks concentrated along bird migration routes. The illness is seasonal, mainly in summer and early autumn, with the peak typically in August–September. Climate conditions—milder winters and hot, humid summers—favor mosquito breeding, helping explain rising numbers in Greece and elsewhere. In Turkey, there is no current outbreak and the situation is not panicked, but authorities remain vigilant due to proximity to affected regions and neighboring Europe. The symptoms resemble flu and are distinguished by the absence of typical respiratory symptoms such as cough or sore throat.

article.articleHeadline: China's SARS-CoV-2 variant outbreak on the rise; prognosis may be similar to that of AIDS patients | China's COVID-19 outbreak | Confirmed cases | Complications.
article.articleSummary: China’s SARS-CoV-2 outbreak is rising, with Omicron lineage PQ.16.1.1 and its sublineages predominant. As of September 2026, China reported 346,000 new confirmed COVID-19 cases, 271 severe cases, and 9 deaths (all with underlying diseases). Local genomic surveillance covered 15,996 sequences, all Omicron. Virologists warn the true infection burden is higher and that severe cases exhibit immune complications; one advocate describes AIDS-like immune exhaustion that can lead to fatal bacterial or fungal infections. On Oct 26, Cao Yunlong’s team published findings that the BA.3.2.2 variant has an immune mechanism favoring transmission in children. They note first vaccine doses leave a lasting immune imprint and domestic vaccines have weak protection, contributing to pediatric infections. Another virologist claims inactivated vaccines may accelerate cancer and diabetes, and cites risks of myocarditis, pericarditis, immune thrombosis, and nerve damage; vaccine discussions are politically sensitive in China. Overall prognosis may resemble AIDS in severe immune dysfunction.

article.articleHeadline: Unbearable back pain in a teenage girl turns out to be a bacterial infection; doctor says invasive procedures should be approached with caution.
article.articleSummary: A 14-year-old girl in Xiamen, Fujian, China, presented with persistent lower back pain but no fever. Imaging revealed destruction of the L4 vertebral body with a suspected paravertebral abscess, indicating spinal infection. Routine blood tests showed normal white blood cell count, but erythrocyte sedimentation rate was markedly elevated; tuberculosis was ruled out. Lumbar lesion biopsy demonstrated abundant Staphylococcus aureus, confirming vertebral osteomyelitis caused by S. aureus. The infection was likely seeded through an invasive procedure performed at a clinic, allowing bacteria to invade the spine. Targeted antibiotics led to rapid pain relief and good recovery on follow-up. The report emphasizes that teenage spinal infections are rare and may present without fever, urging thorough evaluation of persistent or progressive back pain (over ~2 weeks) with ESR and MRI, and caution against early invasive therapies such as acupuncture or local injections. Obtaining tissue for culture is essential to guide precise therapy and prevent chronic complications. Keywords: spinal infection, Staphylococcus aureus, vertebral osteomyelitis, adolescent health, invasive procedures.

article.articleHeadline: Once infected, you carry it for life! This virus has entered a high-incidence period.
article.articleSummary: Varicella-zoster virus reactivation causes herpes zoster (shingles). Autumn–winter is a high-incidence period as reduced immunity promotes reactivation after primary chickenpox infection, with the virus latent in dorsal root ganglia. Shingles progresses through prodrome (low fever, fatigue and local pain), eruption (unilateral belt-like clusters of vesicles with neuralgia), and postherpetic neuralgia (pain lasting months to years). It can affect any nerve innervated site, not only the waist, including head, neck, chest, eyes, ears, and occasionally the face. Do not delay treatment; antiviral therapy within 72 hours of rash onset, plus analgesia, minimizes nerve damage. Transmission occurs via vesicle fluid; most adults are immune, but unvaccinated children should avoid contact until crusting. Prevention relies on vaccination and maintaining immune health. Information source: National Emergency Broadcast; Dr. Zhu Qian, Pain Department, China-Japan Friendship Hospital, Beijing.

article.articleHeadline: GHS contains yellow fever outbreak after confirming four cases
article.articleSummary: Ghana Health Service (GHS) says it has contained a yellow fever outbreak after confirming four cases recorded between September and the first half of October. The four cases were detected in Sissala West, Wa West, Etu, and Nadowli-Kaleo districts, with samples sent to Dakar, Senegal, for laboratory confirmation, and results subsequently confirmed four infections. Health authorities rolled out vaccination interventions to curb further spread. Speaking on TV3 on November 1, 2026, GHS Director‑General Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea said the outbreak has been curtailed and vaccination campaigns are part of the response. The GHS is also probing reports of deaths in affected communities to determine if they were due to yellow fever, amid ongoing public health measures and surveillance.

article.articleHeadline: Ghana AIDS Commission Launches Youth Desk To Tackle Infections Among Young People
article.articleSummary: Ghana AIDS Commission launches a Youth Desk to tackle HIV infections among young people in Ghana. On 2 November 2026, the Commission introduced the Youth Desk to elevate HIV prevention, awareness, testing and treatment discussions and to involve youth in the national HIV response. The desk aims to improve access to accurate information, promote responsible health decisions, and bridge gaps caused by limited reliable information, stigma and misconceptions. It seeks to strengthen collaboration with youth organizations, educational institutions and other stakeholders to foster open conversations about sexual health, promote voluntary HIV testing, early diagnosis and treatment access, and reduce new infections by empowering young people with education and services.

article.articleHeadline: Warning about the emergence of a new influenza strain. Doctors warn of the risk posed by a dangerous virus. Who is most at risk.
article.articleSummary: Thousands of Scots are urged to vaccinate against influenza amid fears of a new devastating strain. Health experts warn a viral mutation could cause severe disease and even spark a new pandemic. The scenario involves influenza viruses circulating in animals and humans mixing to produce a dangerous, immune-evasion variant. Scottish scientists emphasize workers in close contact with live animals—farmers, agricultural workers, veterinarians, inspectors, animal transport drivers, and abattoir staff—face heightened risk and should receive the flu shot. The NHS in the UK provides free vaccination to vulnerable groups to reduce infection risk. The alert follows reports of a Brazilian woman’s death from swine flu in recent weeks, with additional avian influenza cases in China and Cambodia. Authorities stress animal-origin viruses rarely transmit human-to-human, but co-infection could favor a highly contagious novel variant; the risk is theoretical but being monitored.

article.articleHeadline: Tragedy in Brazil: A four-month-old infant died of meningitis, 36 people received prophylactic treatment.
article.articleSummary: Four-month-old infant died in Pouso Alegre, Minas Gerais, Brazil, from confirmed meningococcal meningitis serogroup C. The child was unvaccinated. After confirmation, health authorities traced 36 close contacts (family members and healthcare workers) and provided prophylactic treatment to curb transmission. Meningococcal meningitis is a serious bacterial infection causing inflammation of the brain and spinal cord membranes and can progress rapidly, potentially fatal within hours. In infants, symptoms may be nonspecific—irritability, drowsiness, and poor feeding—while older individuals experience fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, and altered consciousness. Authorities promote vaccination, part of Brazil’s national immunization program, offered free through the public SUS. Emphasis is placed on adhering to vaccination schedules and seeking prompt medical evaluation for suspected meningitis to prevent severe outcomes or further spread.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue: Child deaths in Peru already exceed those recorded for all of 2025, according to MINSA records.
article.articleSummary: By Oct 24, 2026, Peru reports 16,224 dengue cases in children aged 0–11, doubling 2025’s 8,067. MINSA records 23 pediatric deaths, exceeding all of 2024 (18) and 2025 (16). San Martín leads with 7 child deaths (ages 3–11), followed by Piura (5), Ucayali (3), and Lambayeque, Madre de Dios (2 each), with Amazonas, Junín, La Libertad, and Loreto each recording one. Children account for about 25% of nationwide dengue fatalities. Automedication is a recurring risk factor, with many families opting for private clinics or medications, delaying proper care. Dengue serotype 3 has circulated across nearly all regions since 2025, associated with faster replication and stronger inflammatory responses, increasing severity. El Niño conditions raise Aedes aegypti breeding, likely elevating cases in coming months. Authorities urge early warning recognition and timely health care, and call for pharmacy regulation to curb unsafe treatments.

article.articleHeadline: Brazil: São Paulo reports four cases of hantavirus infection so far this year
article.articleSummary: Four hantavirus infections have been confirmed in São Paulo state this year, with one death, per a Oct 26 alert by SES-SP highlighting a high fatality risk. Hantavirus infection, transmitted by wild rodents, can lead to heart and respiratory failure. Since 2007, São Paulo has 199 cases and 101 deaths (case fatality ~50.8%), higher than Brazil’s national CFR ~46.5%. As of Sep 2026, four local cases are recorded. Primary reservoirs in Brazil are the rice rat (Oligoryzomys) and Necromys lasiurus (field mouse) in the Cerrado. Although globally rare, hantavirus disease is typically severe in Brazil, with most patients requiring hospital care. From 1993–Mar 2026, Brazil reported about 2,400 cases and ~960 deaths; peak activity occurred 2004–2011, with CFRs up to 53%. Most activity is in the South, Southeast, and Central-West; 16 of 27 states have hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, affecting rural, male adults 20–39 through exposure to rodents or contact with their habitats.

article.articleHeadline: Men account for the majority of severe acute respiratory syndrome cases.
article.articleSummary: In Acre, Brazil, Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SRAG) in 2026 totals 1,651 confirmed cases with 46 deaths, incidence 187.48, updated to October 26, 2026. Men account for 56% of SRAG cases and women 44%. Age distribution shows 65+ with 150 women and 132 men; 50–64 with 60 women and 56 men; 15–49 with 100 men and 94 women; 5–14 with 102 boys and 81 girls; 2–4 with 133 boys and 89 girls. Racial distribution is predominantly pardos (83.8%), Indigenous 11%, White 3.8%, Black 0.8%, Asian 0.2%, and 0.4% unknown. Detected respiratory viruses in early 2026 weeks among hospitalized SRAG patients include RSV and rhinovirus; deaths are associated with influenza A(H1N1), metapneumovirus, adenovirus, bocavirus, and COVID-19. Geographic focus: Acre state, Brazil, with ongoing monitoring of demographic and etiologic patterns.
